cases.name: and-or-sequence-pipe
cases.why: Every control operator between commands separates simple commands, listed in source order.

cases.name: subshell-parentheses
cases.why: A subshell's parentheses are not words, and the commands inside are listed in order.

cases.name: brace-group-closing-brace-and-redirection
cases.why: A closing brace is not a word and is not listed, and a redirection and its target are removed before the argv is formed.

cases.name: sudo-u-wrapper
cases.why: sudo, its -u option and that option's argument are stripped.

cases.name: sudo-mixed-options
cases.command: sudo -E -u ncenter -H git push origin feat/x
cases.why: sudo options with and without arguments are all stripped, in any order.

cases.name: env-assignments
cases.command: env A=1 B="x y" git status --short
cases.why: env and the assignments after it are stripped, including one whose quoted value holds a space.

cases.name: timeout-duration
cases.why: timeout and its duration are stripped.

cases.name: stacked-wrappers
cases.command: sudo -u ncenter env GIT_TRACE=1 timeout 30 git checkout main
cases.why: Wrappers in a row are stripped one after another.

cases.name: nice-nohup-command-exec
cases.command: nice git fetch; nohup ./run.sh > log 2>&1 & command git status; exec git log -1
cases.why: nice, nohup, command and exec are each stripped, and a trailing & separates commands like ;.

cases.name: git-global-options-kept
cases.why: git's own global options are arguments, not wrappers, and stay in the argv.

cases.name: design-cd-then-git-dash-c-checkout
cases.why: The design's checkout line splits into two simple commands with git's -C kept in place.

cases.name: leading-assignments-with-expansion
cases.why: Leading assignments are stripped from the argv, but an expansion inside one is still reported.

cases.name: assignment-only-command-omitted
cases.why: A command that is only assignments yields no simple command and is not listed, but the substitution inside it is.

cases.name: if-then-else-fi
cases.command: if git diff --quiet; then git merge --ff-only b; else echo dirty; fi
cases.why: if, then and else are stripped from the front of their commands, and the closing fi is not a command.

cases.name: while-not-time-until
cases.command: while ! git fetch -q; do sleep 1; done; time cargo build; until true; do :; done
cases.why: while followed by !, do, time and until are all stripped, and done is not a command.

cases.name: keywords-as-arguments
cases.command: echo if then do else fi done
cases.why: Keywords are stripped only at the start of a command, never from the arguments.

cases.name: for-loop-header
cases.command: for p in $pids; do kill $p; done
cases.why: A loop header is itself a simple command, whose words are for, the variable, in, and the list. That is where a list is written, and a list is what one rule reads.

cases.name: for-loop-quoted-list-multiline
cases.command:
for x in "$L"
do
  echo "$x"
done
cases.why: Quote removal makes "$L" the same argv word as $L, so only the expansion's context tells a quoted list from a bare one, and a do alone on its line leaves nothing to list.

cases.name: nested-command-substitution
cases.why: An argv word keeps a substitution's source text verbatim, and nested substitutions are listed in the source order of their opening delimiters, outermost first.

cases.name: expansion-context-innermost
cases.why: Every expansion takes the context of the innermost construct enclosing it, so a bare name inside a substitution is cmdsub and a double-quoted name inside that substitution is dquote again.

cases.name: backticks
cases.why: A backtick body is a command substitution whose command is listed after the command containing it.

cases.name: backticks-expansion-inside
cases.why: An expansion inside backticks has the cmdsub context.

cases.name: heredoc-unquoted
cases.why: An unquoted heredoc body is not a command, but its expansions are reported with the heredoc context.

cases.name: design-heredoc-quoted-macro
cases.why: A single-quoted delimiter yields no expansions from the body, so the macro fragment reports nothing.

cases.name: heredoc-double-quoted-delimiter
cases.why: A double-quoted delimiter yields no expansions.

cases.name: heredoc-backslash-delimiter
cases.why: A backslash-quoted delimiter is a quoted delimiter and yields no expansions.

cases.name: heredoc-partly-quoted-delimiter
cases.why: Quoting any part of the delimiter makes it quoted, and the body ends at the plain spelling EOF.

cases.name: heredoc-dash-tab-stripped
cases.why: The <<- form ends at a tab-indented delimiter and still expands its body.

cases.name: heredoc-body-quotes-are-literal
cases.why: Quotes in an unquoted heredoc body are ordinary characters, so both names expand with the heredoc context, while a backslash still escapes $K.

cases.name: heredoc-operator-line-continues
cases.command:
cat <<EOF | grep -c x; echo "$A"
$B x
EOF
cases.why: Commands after the heredoc operator on the same line come before the body in source order.

cases.name: two-heredocs-one-line
cases.why: Two heredocs on one line take their bodies in order, and only the unquoted one yields an expansion.

cases.name: heredoc-body-command-substitution
cases.command:
W=.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-31-operator-console-plan; cat >> $W/progress.md <<EOF
- Operator, $(TZ='Asia/Seoul' date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M KST'): **this session stops after T4**
EOF
echo ok
cases.why: A heredoc whose delimiter is unquoted is live: measured on this host, its command substitution runs, so its command is listed like any other.

cases.name: heredoc-delimiter-as-line-prefix
cases.why: A body line that only begins with the delimiter does not end the heredoc.

cases.name: heredoc-unterminated
cases.why: Measured on this host: the shell reads an unterminated heredoc's body to the end of the input and runs it, so this is a body and not a parse error. An unterminated quote still is one.

cases.name: here-string
cases.why: <<< is a here-string, not a heredoc, so its word is read on the same line and no body follows.

cases.name: comments
cases.why: A word-initial # starts a comment in which an apostrophe opens no quote, a # inside a word is literal, and $# is a special parameter that is not reported.

cases.name: escaped-dollar-forms
cases.why: A backslash escapes the dollar sign outside and inside double quotes, but an escaped backslash leaves the following $L live.

cases.name: ansi-c-quoting
cases.why: $'...' interprets its escapes and expands no parameter.

cases.name: single-inside-double-and-reverse
cases.why: Single quotes inside double quotes do not stop expansion, and double quotes inside single quotes do not start it.

cases.name: design-bash-c-single-quoted
cases.why: The pipeline inside a single-quoted argument is one argv word, not a simple command, and yields no expansion.

cases.name: braced-forms-name-and-next
cases.why: For a braced form the name stops at the first non-name character inside the braces, and next starts there.

cases.name: braced-unbraced-records-collide
cases.why: The two produce the same name and the same following characters, which is why the record also carries whether it was braced -- one rule denies the unbraced form and allows the braced one, and nothing else separates them.

cases.name: zsh-flag-and-length-forms
cases.command: set -- ${=spec}; for p in ${(f)pids}; do :; done; echo ${#PIPESTATUS[@]}
cases.why: The record names the parameter actually named, with a leading # and any parenthesised flag group skipped, and keeps the flags themselves, because one rule must allow a split that was asked for while denying one that was not.

cases.name: positional-parameters
cases.why: A digit after the dollar sign is reported as the name, braced or not.

cases.name: special-parameters-not-reported
cases.why: Special parameters are neither a NAME nor a digit, so none is reported.

cases.name: arithmetic-is-not-substitution
cases.why: $(( )) is arithmetic, not a command substitution, and the bare n inside it is not a dollar expansion.

cases.name: paren-inside-quotes-inside-substitution
cases.why: A closing parenthesis inside quotes within $( ) does not end the substitution.

cases.name: line-continuation
cases.why: A backslash-newline joins two lines into one simple command.

cases.name: unterminated-double-quote
cases.why: An unterminated double quote is a parse error, which callers read as allow.

cases.name: unterminated-single-quote-on-later-line
cases.why: An unterminated single quote on any line makes the whole command a parse error, the valid line before it included.

cases.name: unterminated-command-substitution
cases.why: An unterminated $( is a parse error in zsh.

cases.name: unterminated-backtick
cases.why: An unterminated backtick is a parse error in zsh.

cases.name: redirection-targets
cases.why: Redirection operators and their targets are not argv words, but an expansion in a target is still reported.

cases.name: brace-expansion-is-not-a-group
cases.why: A { attached to other characters is an ordinary word, and only a standalone { is the group keyword.

cases.name: export-path-list
cases.why: An assignment-looking word after a command name is an argument, and both expansions in it are reported.

cases.name: bash-c-double-quoted
cases.why: A double-quoted argument handed to another shell is one argv word whose expansion zsh still performs.

cases.name: single-quoted-substitution-text
cases.why: $( inside single quotes is text, not a command.

cases.name: negation-assignment-wrapper-mixed
cases.why: A keyword, an assignment and a wrapper are stripped in the order they appear.

cases.name: xargs-is-not-a-wrapper
cases.why: xargs is not in the wrapper list, so its argv keeps xargs first.

cases.name: next-crosses-an-operator
cases.why: next is the raw three characters after the name even where & ends the word, so a consumer must not read :g& here as a modifier.

cases.name: design-cmdsub-assignment
cases.why: The design's modifier line has an assignment-only outer command and one inner command whose expansion is in the cmdsub context.

cases.name: design-heredoc-pipestatus
cases.why: The design's PIPESTATUS heredoc line reports one braced expansion with the heredoc context.

cases.name: corpus-loop-with-substitution-assignments
cases.command: for c in b594ee7 4f85b5f; do n=$(git show $c:crates/godo-config/src/tracker.rs | grep -c '#\[godo('); r=$(git show $c:crates/godo-config/src/tracker.rs | grep -c 'range *='); echo "$c  declared=$n  ranged=$r  undeclared=$((82-n))"; done
cases.why: A real loop whose assignment-only commands each hide a two-stage pipeline, with a # inside single quotes and expansions in both cmdsub and dquote contexts.

cases.name: corpus-quoted-python-heredoc-then-loop
cases.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
import pathlib,re
for rev in ("before","after"):
    pass
EOF
for rev in 82e9def~1 82e9def; do
  o=$(git show $rev:crates/godo-lidar/src/dense.rs | grep -E '^\s*//' | grep -o '(' | wc -l)
done
cases.why: A real quoted Python heredoc whose body holds a Python for line, then a shell loop, so the body must not be read as commands.

cases.name: corpus-bare-lease-push-with-zsh-pipestatus
cases.command: git push --force-with-lease origin feat/issue-175-journal-panel 2>&1 | tail -4; echo "PUSH_EXIT=${pipestatus[1]}"; echo "=== ahead of main ==="; git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD
cases.why: A real push whose redirection and pipe are split out, with the zsh pipestatus spelling inside double quotes.

cases.name: corpus-timeout-grep-or
cases.command: timeout 300 cargo fmt -p godo-localizer-lidar -- --check 2>&1 | head -30; echo "FMT-EXIT:${PIPESTATUS[0]}"; echo "--- probe residue check ---"; grep -n "TEMPORARY T4 PROBE\|t4_probe_numbers\|REMOVE BEFORE HANDOVER" bins/godo-localizer-lidar/src/compute.rs || echo "none"; echo "--- git status ---"; git status --short
cases.why: A real gate line with a timeout wrapper, || and a double-quoted pattern whose backslashes stay because they escape nothing there.

cases.name: corpus-conflict-markers-inside-nested-quotes
cases.command: for f in $R $D; do echo "  $f: open/base/close=$(grep -cE '^(<<<<<<<|\|\|\|\|\|\|\||>>>>>>>)' $f)  '=======' here=$(grep -cx '=======' $f) main=$(git show origin/main:$f | grep -cx '=======') branch=$(git show f552d04:$f | grep -cx '=======')"; done
simple_commands: $f: open/base/close=$(grep -cE '^(<<<<<<<|\|\|\|\|\|\|\||>>>>>>>)' $f)  '=======' here=$(grep -cx '=======' $f) main=$(git show origin/main:$f | grep -cx '=======') branch=$(git show f552d04:$f | grep -cx '=======')
cases.why: A real line where <<<<<<< sits in single quotes inside $( ) inside double quotes, so it must not open a here-string or heredoc.

cases.name: corpus-heredoc-operator-then-and
cases.command:
git status --short && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -1
feat(issue#221): the target link is a step somebody performs, and now something says so

`git worktree add` creates no `target` symlink, nothing warns, and the build
succeeds — onto the SD card the arrangement exists to protect. One worktree made
on 2026-09-09 put **4.4 GB** there in its first `--workspace` gate.
MSG
cases.why: A real commit whose heredoc operator is followed by && on the same line, so the command after it is listed before the body ends.

cases.name: braced-flag-distinguishes-the-two-spellings
cases.why: The two differ in nothing a caller can see except the braced flag, and one rule denies the first and allows the second.

cases.name: flags-are-kept-so-a-requested-split-is-visible
cases.why: A split that was asked for is allowed and one that was assumed is not, so the flag has to survive into the record.

cases.name: parenthesised-flag-group-is-skipped-to-the-name
cases.why: The parameter actually named is pids, and the flag group is what says the split was requested.

cases.name: length-form-names-the-parameter-not-the-hash
cases.why: The rule reads the parameter named, not the characters the expansion begins with, so the length form is the same defect in another spelling.

cases.name: position-points-at-the-dollar
cases.why: A caller that reports what it matched needs where it was, and the position is the dollar rather than the name.
